name: Behavioral Activation - 1
description: The key idea here is that doing more of what matters changes how you feel, rather than waiting to feel better first. For one day, write down what you do and rate each activity for enjoyment and importance. Do not try to change anything yet.

steps.prompt: Depression tends to follow a pattern of behavior: withdrawing, avoiding, and doing less of what matters. This approach changes behavior first, because energy, motivation, and mood tend to follow action rather than lead it. Today you only notice your patterns.

Rate each activity twice on a 0 to 10 scale. Enjoyment is how much fun or pleasure it gives you. Importance is how much it matters to you in your heart. An activity can be high in one and low in the other.
List what you did today, as completely as you can, including small things like sleeping or watching TV.
Overall, how was your mood today? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: Today was only about noticing. There was nothing to fix and no right answers, just a clearer look at an ordinary day.
next_note: Nothing to do until you're ready. The next page is about what matters to you.

name: Behavioral Activation - 2
tag: Behavioral activation · Life areas and values
description: Go through five areas of life. In each, say what you value, then list activities that would put that value into practice. Values come first and activities come second.

steps.prompt: Look back at your last daily monitoring. Which activities were enjoyable, which were important, which were both, and which were neither? Don't change anything yet. Just notice.

A life area is a part of your life. A value is how you want to live in that area, and it should be your own. An activity is something you can actually do that lives out that value. Activities must be observable by others, measurable, and broken into the smallest possible piece. 'Feeling better' is not an activity. 'Eating dinner with my mother twice a week' is.
Relationships (family, friends, partner): what do you value here?
Relationships: which activities would live out those values?
Education/career: what do you value here?
Education/career: which activities would live out those values?
Recreation/interests (fun, relaxing, helping others): what do you value here?
Recreation/interests: which activities would live out those values?
Mind/body/spirituality (physical and mental health, faith): what do you value here?
Mind/body/spirituality: which activities would live out those values?
Daily responsibilities (obligations and belongings): what do you value here?
Daily responsibilities: which activities would live out those values?

closing_note: You put words to what matters to you in five parts of your life. None of it has to be perfect or final, and it can change as you do.
next_note: The next page picks from this list, so it's worth coming back when you have a little time.

name: Behavioral Activation - 3
description: Choose 15 activities from your inventory and rank them from easiest to hardest. You won't start any of them in this quest. The point is to have a ladder ready.

steps.prompt: Pick activities across several life areas, because relying on one area narrows your chances of positive experiences. Include some you already do and want to do more, a mix of enjoyable and important ones, and only a few small steps toward big long-term goals.
Choose 15 activities from your inventory. Each should be observable, measurable, in its smallest piece, and tied to a value.
Rank them from 1 (easiest to accomplish) to 15 (hardest). One way: place the easiest as 1 and the hardest as 15, then fill in the rest.

closing_note: You sorted fifteen activities from easiest to hardest. You don't have to do any of them yet. The ladder is just ready when you are.
next_note: The next page takes the first rung and gives it a day and a time.

name: Behavioral Activation - 4
description: Pick one to three of your easiest activities and give each a specific day and time this week. Think through what might get in the way first.

steps.prompt: Start with one to three of your easiest activities and challenge yourself without getting overwhelmed. Planning a specific day and time makes it more likely to happen. If an activity feels too big, it may not be in its smallest piece yet.
Which one to three activities from your ranking will you start with?
What could get in the way of each one? If there is a barrier, what smaller step could you take first?
Choose a specific day and time for each activity this week.
Through the week, keep logging as in the first quest. Mark each planned activity you complete and rate its enjoyment and importance. If you miss one, replan it for another time that week.

closing_note: You turned an idea into a plan: a day, a time, and what might get in the way. If a plan slips, you can move it. A missed time is information, not a failure.
next_note: Through the week, keep logging what you do, the way you did on the first page. Come back for the next page when the week is up.

name: Behavioral Activation - 5
description: Review last week's planned activities, then choose one hard activity and name up to three people who could support you with it, plus exactly how and when each can help.

steps.prompt: How many of last week's planned activities did you complete?
For those you completed, how easy or hard were they, and how did it feel to do them?
For those you missed, what happened? Was it not enjoyable or important to you, too big, or out of time? Decide whether to swap it, shrink it, or reschedule it.

Sometimes the people around you want to help but don't know how, or they help in ways that don't work for you. A contract is a plan for asking for the specific help you need. Support is meant to make your activities easier, not to replace your own effort. You stay responsible for your activities even if someone doesn't follow through.
Which activity from your list is hard to do on your own?
Name up to three people who could help, and describe exactly how and when each could help.
Next, tell each person what you're trying to do and how they can help. You can show them this plan or just talk it through. Then plan next week's activities, adding one or more new ones.

closing_note: You looked back on your week and asked for help in a specific way. Asking for support is part of the plan, not a sign the plan is falling short.
next_note: When you're ready, plan next week and add one or two new activities.

name: Steady Ground - 1
theory: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, 2nd ed., Mindfulness: Wise Mind (Handout 3)
description: Look at one recent moment through three states of mind: reasonable, emotional, and wise. You're not trying to fix anything, just noticing which one was in charge.

steps.prompt: Your mind moves between three states. Reasonable mind runs on facts and logic. Emotion mind is led by feelings and urges, and often doesn't stop to think about consequences. Wise mind is the balance of the two, a calm, centered place that looks out for your long-term wellbeing. Everyone has a wise mind, even people who haven't found it yet.
Think of a recent moment when you reacted strongly or felt pulled in two directions. What was happening?
In that moment, which state was running things? The middle is wise mind.
If your wise mind had a say, what would it tell you about that moment?
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: You looked at a real moment and asked which part of you was driving. No state is wrong. Each one just has a different job.
next_note: The next page practices two skills for noticing what's happening inside you.

name: Steady Ground - 2
theory: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, 2nd ed., Mindfulness module: 'what' skills (observe, describe)
description: Practice two skills: noticing without reacting, then putting plain words to what you notice. Stick to facts, not guesses.

steps.prompt: Observe means noticing what's here, inside and outside you, without reacting or trying to change it. Describe means putting words to it using only the facts. A description doesn't add worst-case guesses or leave out what's uncomfortable. A thought is just a thought, and a feeling is just a feeling.
Take one minute just to notice. What do you see, hear, and feel in your body right now? Write it down without judging it.
Pick one feeling you noticed. Describe it using facts only, like 'I notice a tightness in my chest' or 'I notice the thought that I'm behind.' Where is it, and what thought is attached to it?
How strong is that feeling right now?
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: You noticed what was here and named it without arguing with it. That small gap between feeling something and reacting to it is what the next page builds on.
next_note: The next page uses that gap in a moment when you feel like reacting.

name: Steady Ground - 3
theory: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, 2nd ed., Distress Tolerance: The STOP Skill (Handout 4)
description: Replay a moment when you reacted fast and wished you hadn't, this time with four steps: Stop, Take a step back, Observe, Proceed mindfully.

steps.prompt: STOP is a pause button for moments when you feel like reacting right away. S: Stop. Freeze instead of acting. T: Take a step back, take a break, and take a breath. O: Observe what's happening inside you (thoughts, feelings) and around you. P: Proceed mindfully, and ask whether what you're about to do will make things better or worse. This quest is practice for everyday moments. If you're in crisis, use the help links in your profile.
Think of a recent time you reacted fast and wished you hadn't, like snapping at someone, sending a message, or giving up on something. What happened?
Replay it with STOP. Where could you have paused? What would you have noticed in your thoughts, your feelings, and the room around you?
What would proceeding mindfully have looked like? Which choice would have made things better instead of worse?
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: You rehearsed a pause. It doesn't have to work every time, and each practice makes the pause a little easier to find.
next_note: The next page is about a different kind of pause: accepting something you can't change.

name: Steady Ground - 4
theory: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, 2nd ed., Distress Tolerance: Radical Acceptance, Turning the Mind, Willingness (Handouts 11-13)
description: Pick one small thing you've been fighting that you can't change right now. Separate what's out of your control from what's in it, and choose one willing step.

steps.prompt: Radical acceptance means acknowledging what is, as it is, even when you don't like it. It isn't approval, and it isn't giving up. Pain is part of life, but fighting reality can add suffering on top of it. Accepting is a choice you may need to make again and again. Pick something small and everyday for this quest, not your hardest memory.
What's something small you've been fighting that you can't change right now?
What about it is outside your control?
What is inside your control, like your thoughts, your actions, or how you respond?
Write one sentence you could say to yourself to turn toward acceptance. You may need to say it more than once.
What's one willing step you could take, just what the situation needs and nothing more?
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: Accepting something doesn't mean you like it. It means you've stopped spending energy on arguing with it, so you have more for what you can do.
next_note: The last page is about changing how you feel by changing what you do.

name: Steady Ground - 5
theory: Linehan (2015), DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, 2nd ed., Emotion Regulation module: Opposite Action
description: Every emotion comes with an urge. Pick one emotion that's been pulling at you, name its urge, and plan one small action in the opposite direction.

steps.prompt: Emotions push you to act, and acting on the push can strengthen the emotion. Opposite action means doing the reverse. When you feel fear and want to avoid, approach the thing you're afraid of in a small step. When you feel sad and want to withdraw, get active and connect with someone. When you feel angry and want to attack, gently step away, slow down, breathe, and do something kind.
Which emotion has been pulling at you lately, and what does it urge you to do?
How strong is that emotion right now?
What's one small action that goes the opposite way from that urge?
When and where could you do it in the next day or two?
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: You named an urge and planned one small step in the other direction. After you try it, notice whether the feeling shifts at all, even a little.
next_note: Come back to this one any time an emotion is pushing you around.

name: Breathing Space
theory: Segal, Williams & Teasdale (2013), Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression, 2nd ed., three-minute breathing space
description: A short pause with three steps: notice what's here, gather your attention on your breath, then widen your awareness to your whole body. Use it any time you notice you're on autopilot or something feels hard.

steps.prompt: Before you start, how would you describe your mood? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)
This takes about three minutes, roughly one minute per step. The three steps spell AGE: Awareness, Gathering, Expanding. It doesn't fix anything. It makes a little room around whatever is going on.

Step 1, Awareness (about one minute). Sit or stand upright, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Ask yourself, 'What is my experience right now?' Notice any thoughts, treating them as passing events. Notice any feelings, including uncomfortable ones. Notice any sensations in your body, like tightness or bracing. You don't need to change anything.
What did you notice? (optional)

Step 2, Gathering (about one minute). Gently bring all your attention to your breath. Feel your belly rise as you breathe in and fall as you breathe out. If your mind wanders, bring it back without criticizing yourself.

Step 3, Expanding (about one minute). Widen your attention from your breath to your whole body, your posture, and your face. Let whatever is here be here. When you're ready, carry this wider awareness into the next moments of your day.
How would you describe your mood now? (0 is most negative, 10 is most positive)

closing_note: You paused and noticed what was here. Nothing needed to change for that to count.
next_note: Come back any time. It works best when you use it often, not only when things are hard.
